title: Editors and Reading Errors
description: What an IDE does for you, and how to read a Java error message instead of fearing it.

content.value: An **IDE** (Integrated Development Environment) is an editor built for programming. IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse and VS Code are popular for Java.

content.real: A workshop with every tool on the wall
content.text: You could write Java in any plain text editor and compile by hand. An IDE does the boring parts for you, so mistakes are cheaper to find.

content.value: The editor beside this lesson is a small IDE. It still can't stop every mistake, so reading error messages is the skill that matters.
A **compile error** means `javac` refused to translate your code, so nothing ran. Read the message in order: where, then what.

content.title: First things first

content.value: A **runtime error** is different. The code compiled, the program started, and then something went wrong part way through.

steps.note: This line works, so `Starting up.` prints.
Dividing by zero is something Java cannot do. The program stops with `java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero`, `at Main.main(Main.java:4)`.

content.title: It started, then stopped
content.outro: Some output appeared before the error, so it is a runtime error, not a compile error.

items: The word after `java.lang.` is the **kind** of problem.
The line starting `at Main.main` says **where** it happened.
Those two pieces are usually all you need. Ignore the rest at first.
content.title: Reading it

content.question: Your program prints two lines, then shows an error. What kind of error is it?
options: A compile error
A missing semicolon
A runtime error
Not an error
content.explain: If anything printed, the code compiled and started. It broke while running, so it is a runtime error.

content.title: When an error appears
content.caption: Change one thing at a time. If you change four things and the error goes away, you learn nothing about which one mattered.

output: Break me, then read the message.
content.caption: Fast programmers aren't the ones who avoid errors. They read them properly the first time.

content.question: You change four things at once and the error goes away. What is the problem?
options: You don't know which change fixed it
Nothing, that is the fastest way
The program will no longer compile
Java undoes your changes
content.explain: Change one thing, run, and read. That way you learn exactly what each error means.

quiz.question: What is a compile error?
options: A mistake found before the program runs, so nothing runs.
A mistake that only happens on slow computers.
A mistake that appears halfway through running.
quiz.explain: `javac` checks first. If it reports an error, no bytecode is produced and the program never starts.

quiz.question: Java says `Main.java:7: error: ';' expected`. Where do you look?
options: Line 7, and the end of line 6 above it.
The first line of the file.
Anywhere: the line number is a rough guess.
quiz.explain: The line number is exact. A missing semicolon is often reported on the line after the one that is missing it, so check the line above too.

quiz.question: Your program prints two lines and then shows an error. What kind of error is it?
options: A runtime error: it compiled and started, then broke.
A compile error: the code never compiled.
Both at once.
quiz.explain: Output appearing proves the code compiled and the JVM started it. Anything that goes wrong after that is a runtime error.

quiz.question: You have fifteen errors after one small change. What is the best next step?
options: Fix the first one and compile again.
Fix the last one, since it is the newest.
Undo everything you have written today.
quiz.explain: Errors cascade: one missing brace confuses everything after it. Fixing the first often clears most of the rest.

quiz.question: What does an IDE do for you?
options: Colours code, spots mistakes early, suggests names, and runs your program.
Writes the program so you do not have to.
Makes errors impossible.
quiz.explain: An IDE shortens the loop between writing and finding out. The thinking, and the reading of error messages, is still yours.
